title: Composite terms named by short collision-free codes
summary: Every term built from the context, including a composite term such as f applied to g of a symbol, receives a code of a fixed small number of bits. Codes never collide and terms that denote the same symbol share a code, so a two-step table chain is answered by decoding one code. A plain address list with a depth counter serves the other tasks.
core_idea: Name every term by an O(1)-bit collision-free code shared by terms that denote the same symbol, and answer chained tables by decoding the code of the composite term.

state.name: A
state.meaning: Address list: C rows of (address symbol, stored symbol), C = 64.

state.name: h
state.meaning: Waiting left symbol of an incoming pair, or empty.

state.name: lvl
state.meaning: Bracket level counter used with the rows of A as a push-down region.

state.name: kappa
state.meaning: The code register: kappa(tau) is the b-bit code of term tau; b is a fixed constant (b = 8 here) independent of the context size.

state.name: D
state.meaning: Decoder from a code to the output symbol, filled by tallying.

update.latex: h=\varnothing \Rightarrow h \leftarrow x_t;\; \text{else } A_{n_A} \leftarrow (h, x_t),\; n_A \leftarrow n_A + 1,\; h \leftarrow \varnothing
update.plain: pairs are appended to the address list A
update.name: append pair

update.plain: at a probe x_t the composite term f(g(x_t)) formed from the tables in context is given its code, a hash of the term; equal denotations get equal codes and distinct ones never share a code
update.name: term code

update.latex: x_t \text{ opener} \Rightarrow lvl \leftarrow lvl + 1,\; A_{lvl} \leftarrow (lvl, x_t);\; x_t \text{ closer} \Rightarrow lvl \leftarrow lvl - 1
update.plain: brackets use the first rows of A as a push-down region indexed by lvl
update.name: bracket level

readout.latex: \hat{y}_t = D[\kappa_t] \text{ for table chains};\; \hat{y}_t = D'[A[\text{row of } x_t]_1] \text{ otherwise}
readout.plain: a table-chain probe is answered by decoding its code; other probes read the row whose address is x_t (or row lvl for brackets) and map the stored symbol through the learned map D'

learning.description: D and D' are majority maps fitted by a tally over m training items; the routing between code decoding, address reading and the push-down region is picked by best training accuracy.
learning.few_shot_argument: Each code identifies its denotation, so D needs one sighting per output symbol: m = 16 items of 32 probes each cover all 32 symbols at T = 32.

complexity.constants_notes: Appending is O(1); an address read scans at most C rows; the code is a fixed b-bit word, so decoding is one access.

sample_efficiency.mechanism: Collision-free codes make the decoder a one-sighting map.

prediction.statement: From m = 16 training items of two-hop composition with T = 32, the per-query accuracy is at least 0.99.

capabilities.prediction: f(g(x)) at T = 4, 16, 32 with accuracy 1.0, decoding one b-bit code per probe.
Chains of 1, 4, 8 hops by repeated address reads (C = 64).
Exact at K = 8, 32, 64 and L = 8, 32, 64 with C = 64 rows (2C + 2^b + 3 words).
Exact closers at depth 2, 4, 8, 16 from the push-down rows.
The limit is a storage count: C slots of two words cannot hold more than C pairs, so at C = 64 an instance with 65 or more distinct pairs loses one of them.

falsifiers: Two composite terms with different denotations that receive the same b-bit code.
16 training items at T = 32 after which the composition accuracy is below 0.99.

toy_example.description: T = 3 tables; codes are the denoted symbols; decoder is the identity.
